learning_objective: 🎯 Master the art of 'Cloze tests' (Gap Filling) by understanding context, subject-verb agreement, prepositions, and Conjunctions that link ideas logically!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: These connect words, phrases, or independent clauses of equal rank. Remember the acronym FANBOYS: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So. (e.g., 'He is poor, BUT he is honest.')

These always come in pairs and connect equal parts of a sentence. Memorize the pairs: Either...or, Neither...nor, Not only...but also, Both...and, Though...yet, No sooner...than, Hardly/Scarcely...when.

These introduce a dependent clause and show a relationship (Time, Reason, Condition) with the main clause. Examples: Because, Since, As, Although, If, Unless, Until, While. (e.g., 'You will fail UNLESS you study.')

1. Read the whole paragraph first to understand the Context and Tense (Past/Present). 2. Check Subject-Verb Agreement (Singular subject = Singular verb). 3. Look at the words immediately before and after the blank (Prepositions usually follow specific verbs, like 'fond OF', 'listen TO').

fun_activity.title: 👯 Find the Missing Twin
fun_activity.instructions: Correlative conjunctions are twins; they never travel alone! If you see 'Either', its twin 'or' must be nearby. If you see 'Not only', 'but also' is definitely coming! Play a game: whenever you hear 'No sooner', shout 'THAN'! Whenever you hear 'Hardly', shout 'WHEN'!

exam_tips: 📌 'Although' or 'Though' is followed by a comma (,) or 'yet'. NEVER use 'but' after Although! (Correct: 'Though he is rich, yet he is unhappy' or 'Though he is rich, he is unhappy').
📌 'Lest' is always followed by 'should'. (e.g., 'Walk carefully lest you should fall'). It means 'कहीं ऐसा न हो कि'.
📌 In Gap Filling, if the paragraph is a story, it is almost always in the Past Tense. Fill the blanks with V2 or Past continuous.
quick_recap: ⭐ 'Unless' and 'Until' already have a negative meaning. Do not use 'not' with them in the same clause.
⭐ 'And' adds information, 'But' shows contrast, 'So' shows result, and 'Because' shows reason.
⭐ When subjects are joined by 'Either...or' / 'Neither...nor', the verb matches the subject CLOSEST to the verb.
